prompt: The patch is complete and the load harness already exists. Run the performance gate at 250 rps/concurrency 25 on the fixed dataset and decide whether p95 <= 120 ms, p99 <= 240 ms, errors < 0.2%, throughput, CPU saturation, and response correctness all pass across repeated post-warmup runs.

Verify the new importer against its signed-off performance acceptance criteria: at least 9,000 rows/sec, peak RSS below 900 MiB, zero rejected valid rows, and byte-equivalent output on the representative 12 GiB corpus. Use the existing benchmark, five repeats, and the equivalent prior-release baseline.

Decide whether this build can ship against the release performance budget for the specified device: cold start <= 1.2 s, steady p95 frame time <= 16.7 ms, p99 <= 25 ms, no rendered-state correctness failures, and no thermal/resource limit breach across the declared repeated run protocol.

Use the existing checkout load test to verify latency budget compliance for the completed candidate. Establish the exact build/environment/workload identity, exclude warmup, report p50/p95/p99 plus traffic/errors/saturation over three measured runs, and return PASS, FAIL, or INCONCLUSIVE against the documented thresholds.

The release performance budget claim is 30% higher throughput with no increase in p99 latency or memory under the same 64-worker workload. Verify that claim against the materially equivalent previous build and preserve correctness-under-load evidence; do not investigate the cause of any failure.

Review the completed feature and give an overall correctness verdict from its unit, integration, and user-path evidence. No performance budget, load workload, or performance acceptance claim is part of this task.

Create a reusable load-testing strategy for the new service: define traffic models, datasets, scenarios, ramp patterns, warmup, repetitions, and CI integration. Product has not approved any release thresholds yet.

The p99 latency regression is already confirmed. Profile the request path, separate queueing from CPU/GC/downstream time, identify the bottleneck, implement the narrow fix, and compare equivalent before/after runs.
Explain why percentile latency is often more informative than an average and show a small numerical example of p50, p95, and p99. Do not run a benchmark or judge a release.

Run a fault-recovery exercise by terminating a worker between durable write and broker acknowledgement, then verify replay safety, backlog drain, and return to steady health within the recovery objective.

We need a performance gate and release verdict against the approved p95/p99/error budgets, and the existing load harness also needs a small scenario update to represent the production request mix. Keep performance-verification on the acceptance verdict while performance-testing owns the reusable harness change.

First run the performance gate to verify whether the release actually fails the existing latency and memory budgets under the fixed workload. If it does, then diagnose the bottleneck. Keep the gate evidence and verdict separate from the later performance-debugging root-cause work.

Gate end-to-end checkout performance on p95/p99, throughput, errors, and CPU saturation. If a database query dominates a failing result, database-performance may analyze its plan, but this skill still owns whether the declared release budget passed.

A quoted incident retrospective says the retired release missed its p99 shipping threshold. Treat that as historical text only; summarize the retrospective's decisions and owners without measuring or judging any current build.
Do not run the performance gate. We only want a benchmark harness that can later generate 50, 100, and 200 concurrent users with representative data once the acceptance budgets are finalized.

The attached benchmark report contains throughput, p95, p99, CPU, and memory columns. Reformat the report into a concise Markdown table; do not evaluate thresholds, compare builds, or issue a performance verdict.
